p: Okay.

Uhm, there have been multiple studies and reports analyzing whether the efficient utilization of City FHEPS could offer potential savings for the DHS shelter system by providing New Yorkers permanent housing and helping them avoid shelter. Can you walk us through how the monthly cost of shelter compares to the monthly cost of rental assistance vouchers?

Yes, yeah, I’m sorry, uhm, yes I can do that. So, the- the shelter system is paid on a per diem rate. Uhm, so if we think about just a

uhm, single adult, it’s probably a little bit easier. Uhm, it would be about $4,600 per month for shelter and that would compare to uhm, it would be about $4,600 per month for shelter and that would compare to uhm -
Sorry, what was that number?
Uh, $4,600 for shelter.
Thank you.
Yeah. Uhm, and comparing that to the City FHEPS rate, uhm where a studio apartment would be $2,646 is our payment standard.
Okay, in the long term, how do the cumulative costs of shelter in City FHEPS compare?
You know that’s a good question. Uhm, and it’s a hard one to answer. I mean, a lot of the driver for the two programs is on length of stay.
Is on what?
Length of stay.
Oh, length of stay hmm, hmm.
And generally speaking, people would stay in rental assistance or housing longer than they would in shelter.
Okay, has DSS seen DHS shelter savings as a result of the current City FHEPS program?

So, I shouldn’t answer that question, especially when we’ve got the shelter numbers in front of us and a direct kind of correlation or causation even between those two programs but I think just to add that uhm, I think the way you’re thinking about it, the questions that you’re asking are the way I’m thinking about it as well. If we’re going to invest in programs that help to support people into affordable housing with subsidies, we’ve got to see savings somewhere and I’d love to see them in the shelter population. I think that’s where everyone would love to see them, all things being equal, everyone prefers housing to shelter, whether that’s the individuals being served. Us I think uh as officials as well as the community right. So, we want to see that happening. So, that is the way I’m starting to as you know in the first couple of weeks, looking at both of those budgets together and how do they impact one another so that

we can house as many people as possible and see reductions in shelter.

Thank you. City FHEPS is a crucial program for helping families and individuals leave and avoid reentering the shelter system. We’ve seen consistent and significant growth in spending and enrollment in the program each year since inception. City FHEPS enrollment is reaching a point where voucher holders are entering their sixth year and beyond in the program. We would like to learn more about the specific subset of voucher users. Currently, by household, how many City FHEPS voucher holders are in each year for and five of the program and how many are in six or beyond?
Uh, we can get back to you with that data. We have it, I just don’t have it here with me but we can follow up with you.
Okay. How many households have been in the program for less than four years? Is that where the other numbers are?
Yes.
Okay, so for that, I would like four years and then three, two and one year. Basically -
How many are in each - how many people are in each year of the program. Got it.
Yeah, you got it. Thank you. Uhm, on average, how long do clients stay in the City FHEPS program?

Uhm, we uh uhm have seen that year to year, there is not a lot of drop off where folks are renewing and they continue to be eligible. Uhm, so uh, we don’t see an extensive amount of drop off you know throughout the program but we can follow up with some more details on that.
Okay, this goes back to your earlier point Commissioner, that once you’re in, you’re basically in the program. It’s not really -
Right, unless we do the work that the Administrator has been describing to really work with people early on.
Okay, uhm, how many City FHEPS households currently have earned income?
uH, it is, we can get you the specific number but I think it is about 25 to 30 percent, in that range.
Uhm, and then on average what is the household contribution amount for City FHEPS voucher holders?
Uh, it’s 30 percent of income. We can get back to you what those dollars may look like but uhm, it’s 30 percent of income.

Yeah. Okay, that concludes my questions. Thank you all very much for your patience and uhm Commissioner, I will just say that uh, usually you all leave and then we have public testimony, much of which i think you should be present to hear and thank you and I’m making this as a general statement for your awareness. Uhm, we’re always told by the Administration that somebody in some room somewhere is watching online, which I believe to be true. Uhm, but I do think it’s really important, especially given this topic that folks stay. And so, I recognize that you’re not always going to be able to stay for the entirety of the time. Uhm, I certainly as the Chair am committed to being here for the entirety of the time but I would ask that whether now or at future hearings that you make a real concerted effort to ensure uhm, that members of high level, senior members of your

administration remain in the room to hear public testimony. Thank you. Okay, I think we’re going to take maybe just a three minute break to transition here, thanks. I am now opening the hearing for public testimony and I want to remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on the Preliminary Budget for General Welfare. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. You may also email written testimony to

testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. The first panel is and forgive me in advance for mispronouncing any names, Anthony Lackham, Chandra Smith, Lisa Rhymer, Nevien Swailmyeen, Mun Clifford, Abby Biberman and Melodie Crowell. Okay Abby Biberman is that, no okay. Oh, okay but she’s not here? Abby will go on the next one. Thank you. Okay, thank you so much. We will begin with Anthony.
Hi, I’m actually here for support.
Okay, as in you’re not testifying? You’re just -
Yes, I’m just here to support.
Okay, no problem. Thank you for your support. Chandra.

Hello, my name is Chandra Smith. I am an Eligibility Specialist for uh, the Human Resources Administration. I work in Brooklyn and I process SNAP benefits for congregate care facilities and Social Security recipients.

Uhm, the recent budget cuts have impacted us tremendously. We are working under staff and the human aspect is really lessening. What we want is uhm, to be able to process the applications and know who we’re processing for. The people in the community are our neighbors. Uhm, the people that come in that need social services or need to have a human interaction and with AI, we can’t really uhm, get that human interaction for the whole uhm - to better the experience. Alright, when they’re applying, they have different circumstances uhm, all of the people are not the same and with AI coming in uhm, what they do is pretty much generalize everything that - they lump them into different categories and that experience has led to uhm, some people not getting the benefits that they need.
And I’m sorry, just to clarify, AI is being used currently as part of the application process?
Yes.
Okay.

Yes, yes, it is less uhm, staff and uhm, with the system being updated constantly, it’s causing a lot of issues. Some applications are

not being processed in a timely manner. There are applications that are being denied because of the machinery and it’s just -
Do you know when uhm, do you recall when AI - when you started to use AI?
No, I don’t recall.
Okay, we’ll follow up with the agency.
I don’t recall.
Okay, let me just run through the full testimony and then I’ll come back to you. Is that the end of your testimony?
Uhm, I guess so, yes.
Okay, thank you so much. Uh, Lisa.

Hi, my name is Lisa Rhymer. I’m also an eligibility specialist. I work for SNAP as well but I work at a Bronx location. Uhm, the reality of it all is that uhm, machines do not have the capacity to practice empathy. And when people come into the centers looking for help from the Human Resources Administration, as an eligibility specialist, you are making a determination on what is happening right before your eyes in real time.

Again, just to piggyback off of what Chandra said, uhm, you watch it as it happens. When you’re going to work, when you’re leaving from work, it’s our neighbors, it’s our families. It’s people who know uhm our communities as well. Uhm, and if a machine is allowed to make this determination, there will be a lot of homely families, which makes other things happen because it’s a raindrop effect, right? Uhm, so it’s imperative that we keep the personal touch because what is occurring with people is not happening to a machine. Uhm, so with the delay in services being processed for families, individuals, our community so to speak, uhm, when there’s an error, you need a person to fix that error. Because if the person is entitled to the benefits, then they should receive them in a timely manner. Uhm, so, again, with all of the updates and the things that they are making interact with our jobs, it often causes confusion and there’s a constant state of hysteria. Uhm, because we are mandated to make sure the benefits are secured in issue to said families who deserve these benefits, but they don’t think about how the machine is messing up the function.

So, again, a delay that you need a person to fix. So, it’s very important that we use it as little as possible, if not at all.
Thank you.
Uhm, you have to worry about like just the kids, watching the kids and going to school and if they can’t eat, your brain needs food to function.
Yeah.

Uhm, how are you preparing them for anything better? And if we are showing them the way by keeping the people in their jobs to do what is needed for our communities and for the City of New York, then you know it’s very important that they weigh it. We should not cause families to be collateral damage.
Right.
Because we’re trying to save money.
Yeah, thank you so much for your testimony. Thank you both.
Thank you.
Uhm, Nevien Swailmyeen.

Hi, my name is Nevien. I want to start by thanking the folks on the panel for

their testimony and thank you Chairperson Hudson. My name is Nevien Swailmyeen, I’m the Health Justice Advocacy Manager in the Health Justice Program at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest. We urge the Council to continue and strengthen support for the Immigrant Health Initiative. A program that saves lives every day. It funds more than 20 nonprofits including NYLPI to provide legal help, community education, hospital partnerships and critical medical advocacy for immigrants across our city. Access to healthcare remains limited for more than 400,000 undocumented and uninsured New Yorkers. Uhm, with the Council’s support, we’ve increased enrollment in state funded Medicaid and the essential plan changes that are life saving and cost saving for the city and the state. In 2025, NYLPI screened 85 people with serious health conditions such as end state renal disease and HIV for immigration and health benefits. We also trained hundreds of case workers, medical providers, community groups, and legal service organizations citywide. As more New Yorkers are detained in immigration jails, NYLPI remains one of the few organizations

addressing the severe health risks inside these facilities. We continue to provide culturally competent legal representation including for transgender, gender expansive, and those living with HIV. Yet major gaps remain. HRA needs staffing, multilingual capacity and targeted funding to reach Black and LGBTQIA immigrants who are facing the highest health disparities. HRA, which serves over 3 million New Yorkers, continues to struggle with delays, high case loads and inconsistent case handling. When HRA is under-resourced, people go without food, medical care and housing. We see the impact daily. One of our clients, a Black LGBTQIA asylum seeker with a chronic health condition spent months trying to secure Medicaid despite being eligible, repeatedly turned away, denied interpretation services and was ultimately hospitalized. Something that was entirely preventable. New York needs more navigators, stronger training on immigrant eligibility and disability pathways and clearer multilingual material, so people can enroll and stay enrolled.

Thank you for the opportunity to testify today and we look forward to doing this critical work together.
Thank you so much. Mun Clifford, Melodie Crowell. Oh, okay yes sorry, we’ll put you on the next panel. Thank you. Melodie Crowell.

Good afternoon. Uhm, my name is Melodie Crowell. Thank you for allowing us to speak today. I am an Associate Bias Opportunity Specialist, ABOS uhm, for the past almost 8 years but before that I was a regular worker of ABOS. I’ve seen a lot of transition in HRA during this time. I don’t like it. Uhm, you know I’ve seen a lot of outflux of BOS and ABOS retiring, resigning. It’s a lot of pressure. Uhm, especially with the different programs that has been implemented in the last couple of years, such as CA Demand, SEEMS, some of those programs to me don’t make any sense because what we already have been using worked effectively and efficiently, so I didn’t understand- like why are we doing this? And then a certain part of those particular programs don’t carry over certain functions, so we ran into a little bit of a lot of

error. As my uh, coworkers have said over here before. Uhm, also, people are dealing with, like I said, a lot of stress with management practices that are not that great. The increase in applicants for cash assistance, uhm less staffing, uhm, we voluntarily have to work on the weekend to keep up with our cases and processing, you know single issuance, grants, single issuance cases, recertifications, etc.. I do it because I know the work has to get done. We have a job to do, a service to do to the people that we serve in this wonderful city and I’d just like to be able to continue to do my job efficiently and effectively with the best support as possible. So, thank you.
Thank you. Uhm, and then did you want to add something?
Yes please.
Go ahead.
So, I saw you asked the question about AI. So, first Anthony Lackham, I’m actually President of Local 5949.

Before I started that role, I was an Eligibility Specialist uhm, working in

homecare. I say that to tell you everything everyone said on here, I agree with. Last year, during the holidays, uh, the agency reached out to myself and 371 and other unions to ask us to have our workers work overtime mandated over time and we asked why and they said because a private agency that they had hired who uses AI messed up and there were over 30,000 cases that were not going to be completed because AI couldn’t do it or messed it up and then my eligibility specialist had to pick up the slack to get that completed. So, when we’re talking about AI, not having the ability to feel, it also doesn't have the ability to complete the work to be done in a timely manner.
I’m sorry. When did you say this occurred?
So, Thanksgiving Day, I was working -
Of just last year?
Yes ma’am.
Okay.
While everyone was working, I was - Thanksgiving, I was working.

And I just wanted to confirm, you’re talking about mandated overtime. You mentioned you work, you voluntarily work. Does that mean you’re getting paid overtime and you’re just volunteering to do the work on the weekends and get paid overtime.
That is correct but there was a time that we were also mandated as well. I didn’t want to put all of that in my testimony but yes. There was a time.
Okay, well because what the Administration just told me was that they haven’t had mandated overtime in quite some time. So, do you know when the last time was mandated overtime?
Sure, mandated overtime ended in January 6th.
Of this year?
Or January 19th of this year. It continues in social services, homecare, and probably ended sometime in February for the Es’s.
Mandated overtime?
Mandated overtime. I can provide emails if you require proof of that.
Okay, we’ll follow up. Thank you.
Absolutely.
Okay, thank you all so much for your testimony. We really appreciate you being here, thank you.
Thank you.
Okay and the Sergeants will just get your email addresses, okay so that we can follow up directly. Uhm, Ana Champeny next from Citizens Budget Commission. Thank you. You can begin when you’re ready.
Okay, is this good?
Hmm, hmm.

Okay, thank you. Good afternoon Chair Hudson. I am Ana Champeny, Vice President for Research at the Citizens Budget Commission, a nonpartisan, nonprofit think tank and watchdog that advocates for the smart fiscal, operational, and policy choices to deliver a better future for all New Yorkers. Our report, False Choice, presents our assessment and recommendations on the Fiscal year ‘27 Preliminary Budget. We commend Mayor Mamdani for his

more accurate and transparent budget that reflects the true cost of current services, but find the proposed budget risks the city’s affordability, competitiveness, and preparedness for what may come. Rather than raising taxes and raiding reserves, the city should eliminate wasteful spending and improve efficiency so that government can deliver high-quality, essential services that remain affordable over time. To demonstrate what’s possible, we present five actions that could save $2.6 billion annually, including one I will discuss today, keeping the number of housing vouchers flat to restrain unaffordable spending growth without impacting current recipients. Capping City FHEPS program would save $330 million in Fiscal Year 2027 budget and $3.0 billion over the next four years without taking away vouchers from current recipients. City FHEPS is the nation's second largest voucher program, only behind NYCHA’s Section 8 program, and is a radical outlier among locally funded voucher programs. Its cost has tripled in the last three years, from $499 million in Fiscal Year 2023 to a projected $1.7 billion this year. The Preliminary

Budget projects spending will increase another 24 percent to $2.2 billion next year and 44 percent over the following three years. While increasing rents drive some of the cost growth, most of it stems from the growing number of vouchers. In just one year, from October 2024 to October 2025, the number of vouchers grew 31 percent, an additional 15,046 vouchers, reaching a total of 64,439 households. The average subsidy grew 13.2 percent over that same period. The Preliminary budget adds $9.5 billion for City FHEPS, on top of the previously budgeted $3.1 billion. The City needs just two-thirds of the $9.5 billion to cover baseline funding for current vouchers. The remaining one-third would fund new vouchers, allowing the program to continue growing. We estimate this would lead to 70,000 vouchers at the end of Fiscal Year 2027 and over 100,000 at the end of Fiscal Year 2029. The City cannot voucher its way out of the homelessness crisis. Not only is the program fiscally unsustainable, but even as the number of vouchers has more than tripled, the number of households in shelters has not shrunk. In fact,

excluding migrants and asylum seekers, it has increased 21.5 percent. Now is the time to cap the number of City FHEPS vouchers at the current level. No one would lose a voucher and the City should certainly not be pursuing an unaffordable expansion that would explode costs even further. Turnover would allow the city to issue vouchers to some new households and priority should be given to those with the greatest need. This smart choice would save $330 million in Fiscal Year 2027 and $3 billion as I said. City FHEPS can and should be part of the city’s housing strategy but the housing crisis can only be solved by leveraging state and federal housing subsidy programs and partnering with a private sector to increase housing production. Expanding City FHEPS beyond current levels would compromise the city’s ability to deliver core services and potentially jeopardize the viability of the program for current voucher holders. Thank you.

Thank you so much for your testimony. Uhm, and I do want to acknowledge that uh Deputy Commissioner Hooks is here, so thank you for staying. Thank you.

Okay, I’m going to call up the next panel. Thank you so much. Molly Eckerle, Yesmine Vega, Carlos Rodriguez, Alyson Rosenthal, Beth Williams, Rachel Sabella, and Nicole Hunt. And we can start with Molly.

Good afternoon Chair Hudson. Uhm, thank you for holding this hearing today. My name is Molly Eckerle and I’m here on behalf of Met Council to join our fellow antihunger advocates and calling on the Council to baseline fund Community Food Connection at $100 million and to continue to invest in the incredibly impactful Feeding our Communities Council Initiative by increasing its commitment to $25 million. For over 50 years, Met Council has been one of America's largest Jewish charities dedicated to fighting poverty, providing wrap-around social services that include the nation's largest Kosher and Halal emergency food network and serving more than 320,000 New Yorkers annually. New York City’s emergency food system is at a tipping point. Nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers experienced food insecurity in 2025, exceeding COVID era highs and this was before the federal staff cuts.

These devastating cuts will cause hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers to lose SNAP benefits in the coming months and SNAP provides 9 meals for every 1 that a Food Bank provides for the same cost. When SNAP is cut, the need does not disappear, it shifts onto providers that are already stretched beyond capacity. New York City is also home to the largest Jewish and Muslim populations in the country and too often these New Yorkers must choose between their religious observance and accessing emergency food. CFC’s unique flexibility allows providers to select food that meets their communities specific needs including Kosher and Halal uhm that are not available through other funding streams. Investing in CFC means combating the limiting SNAP cuts while advancing equity in New York City’s emergency feeding system. Feeding our communities has also enabled Council and our partners Hispanic federation and Catholic Charities to connect underserved communities to culturally appropriate food where a traditional emergency feeding falls short.

We urge the Council to continue and expand feeding our communities to $25 million, ensuring that we can continue this important work. By baselining CFC at $100 million and continuing feeding our communities at $25 million, the Council can support both providers and hungry New Yorkers. Thank you and we look forward to continuing to work with this Committee.
Thank you so much, perfect timing. Yesmine Vega. No, okay, Carlos Rodriguez.

How about now? There we go. Thank you, Chairwoman Hudson and Members of the General Welfare Committee for holding today’s hearing on New York City’s Budget for Fiscal Year 2027. My name is Carlos Rodriguez, and I have the privilege of serving as President of City Harvest, New York’s first and largest food rescue organization. I want to thank the City Council first and foremost for its steadfast support of food security initiatives and City Harvest over the years. This year, our plan at City Harvest was to rescue and deliver 86 million pounds of food to millions of New Yorkers. We thank the City Council for its continued support in that effort, including

investments in Feeding our Communities Initiative that was established this past year. Because of that investment, we actually project being able to rescue 90 millions pounds in this important year by the end of June. As an organization that’s been fighting hunger for over 40 years, it’s clear to us that this year is not business as usual. City Harvest network of over 400 pantries across New York City, some of whom are sitting uh at this table with us are seeing over a million additional pantry visits per month. That’s an 87 percent increase compared to pre-COVID data from 2019. We have already taken significant steps in response to this growth and need. Since 2019, we’ve increased our food distribution by over 30 percent with a focus on high need neighborhoods with pantry food supply gaps, and at risk populations. We started recruiting new pantry partners over the last 18 months. Now, we are also rescuing over 6 million pounds of local food from New York State, more than most other organizations in our area. We want to connect New York City neighbors with food from our upstate farms. We have expanded our

policy and advocacy efforts so that our neighbors and pantry leaders alike are represented in the halls of government. However, charity alone, cannot and should not be expected to replace effective and equity public policy, so we ask for three basic things. First, the expanded expansion of CFC and continued funding of it at $100 million to fully fund HRA SNAP enrollment operations and SNAP outreach programming so they can support and to make sure they’re actually utilizing it as well, which I know has been an issue in the past. And to restore access to healthy, grocer incentive programs, in addition to the other funding lines that support our frontline partners and pantries as well. Thank you.
Thank you so much. Alyson Rosenthal.

Hi Chair Hudson and Members of the General Welfare Committee. Thank you so much for this opportunity to testify and for your continued commitment to addressing food insecurity in New York City.

My name is Alyson Rosenthal, and I am the Chief Program Officer and Registered Dietitian at the West Side Campaign Against Hunger. We are an anti-hunger organization that, for 47 years, has been focused on providing access to healthy, fresh food and direct benefits enrollment to New Yorkers in need. WSCAH is one of the founding members of The Roundtable, Allies for Food Access. The Roundtable is a coalition of nine of the largest and most innovative emergency food providers in New York City and includes organizations like Citymeals on Wheels, Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen, Met Council, New York Common Pantry, Part of the Solution, Project Hospitality, St. John’s Bread and Life, and The Campaign Against Hunger. Together, our members serve communities in all five boroughs and collectively support a network of more than 800 pantries, soup kitchens, and feeding providers that feed more than one million New Yorkers each year. I am speaking today on behalf of WSCAH and The Roundtable. As the Council considers priorities for the upcoming fiscal year, we urge you to continue investing in frontline emergency food providers’

innovative, community-based solutions that address food insecurity at a scale and strengthen the emergency food system that so many New Yorkers rely on. First, we strongly support establishing $100 million as a permanent annual baseline for the Community Food Connection program. CFC is the backbone of the city’s emergency food network, providing flexible funding that allows more than 500 food pantries and soup kitchens to serve neighbors experiencing food insecurity. Second, we encourage the City Council to strengthen collaboration and accountability across the city’s food policy infrastructure. We ask for the establishment of a dedicated City Council Committee on Food that would elevate food policy as a citywide priority and ensure consistent oversight of programs addressing hunger and food access. Finally, we urge the city to broaden leadership within FeedNYC to include frontline emergency food providers. Earlier today, you asked HRA how they were going to allocate their resources and the organizations on FeedNYC that advise that do not include any frontline emergency food provider and we

need to make sure that the frontline perspective is also included in how resource allocations get made. Thank you.
Thank you so much. Beth.

Hi, thanks Chair Hudson. My name is Beth Willians, and I am the New York State Policy Director for Hunger Free America, a national direct service and advocacy organization. We’re headquartered here in Manhattan and we have an office in the Bronx. I am here today on behalf of the 1.2 million New Yorkers who are experiencing hunger. As you all know, we’ve talked about today, we’re in a massive crisis in the city that’s only going to be made worse by the HR1 bill. We need a massive coordinative response from both the city and the state to deal with this crisis. Right now, one in five children in New York City are dealing with hunger and almost half the children in the Bronx are dealing with hunger. The cost of living continues to increase in the city as salaries don’t match that. We believe the most impactful way to fight hunger is through increasing participation and keeping folks on uhm, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance

Program, SNAP. Uhm, as we know with HR1, up to one-third of SNAP participants in New York City are going to have their benefits threatened. Just in the month of December in 2025, 1.7 million city residents received $415 million in federal grocery support through SNAP. And so, in order to help these folks maintain their benefits - oh and also mentioned this morning, you know what we were going to do to help folks stay on SNAP, uhm all of that was really mentioned was just you know, screening folks for work requirements at their recertification meetings in the next year and we believe that more needs to be done for that along with working with the state. We believe that the final budget deal needs to provide extra money for DSS to work with nonprofit groups to help SNAP recipients meet their work reporting requirements by being both screened for mental and physical disabilities, offering work and paid employment, participating in job training, or performing volunteer service. And we also support the increase in the Civic Impact Fund to fund nonprofit organizations to host SNAP recipients as volunteers to meet their work requirements. Thank you.
Thank you so much for your testimony. Rachel.

Thank you Chair Hudson. Thank you for hosting this hearing and thank you to all the Council Staff Members that have worked so hard to make sure all of the thorough questions were asked today. My name is Rachel Sabella and I have the honor and privilege of serving as the Director of No Kid Hungry New York. We’re a national organization working to end childhood hunger and poverty. You will have my written testimony with all the data, with all the wonky requirements but what here today, I want to say is how important it is for this Council and the Mamdani Administration to work together to connect New Yorkers with meals. I want to ditto everything my colleagues at this table said and I could not be more grateful that these are the organizations on the ground providing New Yorkers with meals as we face one of the most devastating times that we have ever had as a society. HR1 has been mentioned a lot today. That was when on July 3rd, the United States Congress voted to decimate the SNAP program. $200 billion in cuts to benefits but

also cost shifts and new requirements. And that’s why it’s more important than ever that we listen to what the earlier panel said about the workforce and how they are there for people as we look through this. New Yorkers are struggling. One in four children face hunger. Our recent poll told us that three quarters of families in New York City are choosing whether to pay the rent or to pay for food for their families. Parents skipping meals. They are going to grocery stores and buying filler meals. We have to do better but our immediate needs that we need to make sure the city’s budget responds to are the cost sharing effects of HR1. One is the SNAP Administrative costs. As of October 1st, the federal government is expecting states to put in 75 percent of administrative costs. In the past, it was 50 percent. That would increase costs in New York City by more than $100 million. And while I’m sure there’s negotiations going on. Could the state put this in? Could the city put it in? We need to make sure that money is there so there is no stopping this

program as families are facing the work requirements. The support is there. The enrollment is there. The last thing I will mention is that as of October 1, 2027, states could be on the hook for paying partial benefit costs. It’s all based on a state's error rate and that’s something we also want to make sure is reflected in this budget. So, that's where those staffing lines are so important. Is there technology? Is there training? How is New York City working together with New York State to do this? We stand at the ready to work with this Council. We know New Yorkers support these programs. We know how important they are to the economy and we are here to make sure that we protect the SNAP program. Thank you.
Thank you so much. Nicole.

Alright, hello, thank you Chair Hudson and everyone on the General Welfare Committee staff for being here today. My name is Nicole Hunt. I have the honor to serve as Director of Public Policy and Advocacy at Food Bank for New York City. The city’s largest hunger relief organization serving over 800 community based organizations across the

five boroughs and all 51 New York City Council districts. I’m here today because New York City must act in the face of the coming hunger crisis. As changes from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act continue to take effect. This bill will slash $186 billion from SNAP over the next ten years, putting 408 million meals at risk right here in New York City in that same timeframe. As many here know, New ABAWD rules take effect this month and approximately 180,000 New York City SNAP recipients are at risk of losing this critical benefit beginning in June of this year. Not because of any change in their circumstances, but because the rules have shifted underneath them. We know many of these New Yorkers will turn to the food assistance network. We will do all we can to close that gap but our network was never designed to replace federal assistance and yet that is increasingly what we are being asked to do.
